Juvenile ankylosing spondylitis (AS) can be distinguished from adult ankylosing spondylitis (AAS) in several ways. While both diseases are characterized by inflammatory conditions that affect the spine and other joints, there are key differences in how they manifest and present.

In children with juvenile AS, the onset of symptoms often begins with oligoarthritis (affecting a few joints initially), followed by enthesitis (inflammation at the sites where tendons and ligaments attach to bones). This group also experiences more frequent involvement of the hip and knee joints. In contrast, adult AS typically starts with spinal stiffness and pain, which can progress to sacroiliitis (inflammation of the sacroiliac joints) and eventually lead to ankylosis (fusion of joints).

MRI studies in children with juvenile AS have shown that secondary physis disruption (the normal development process of bones) is a hallmark of this condition. This disruption is associated with chondroepiphysial widening and subchondral bone edema.

In contrast, adult AS has a more complex and variable presentation. While it can also involve oligoarthritis and enthesitis, the disease often progresses more slowly in adults. The development of gluten tolerance in adult patients with celiac disease is not directly related to juvenile AS; rather, it may be associated with genetic characteristics, particularly those involving HLA genotypes.

Regarding the prognosis of polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR), a higher pre-proliferation PV (PV) is associated with a prolonged duration of steroid therapy and an increased risk of developing granulomatous myelopathy. Conversely, starting patients on >15 mg prednisolone is linked to a prolonged steroid duration.

In terms of vitamin D deficiency and osteochondritis dissecans (OCD), the data suggest that a vitamin D3 deficiency rather than insufficiency may be involved in OCD lesions. A vitamin D3 substitution may help prevent or delay the development of advanced OCD stages. However, more research is needed to confirm these findings.

Lastly, regarding adult body circumferences and height, it has been shown that these measurements scale significantly from one dimension to another across various populations.
